newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Christianity a potent social force in U.S..
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Christianity a potent social force in U.S..

text.p: (This is the first of five articles on aspects of Christianity in the United States where fundamentalism is a potent political and social force. Other articles will run this week and early next week.)
By Alan Elsner

The telephone directory for Lynchburg, a town of 70,000 people in the shadow of the Blue Ridge mountains in southern Virginia, lists no fewer than 236 Christian churches divided into 49 denominations.
Baptists alone can choose to worship at the churches of Mt. Carmel, Mt. Evergreen, Mt. Moriah, Mt. Obed, Mt. Peeler, Mt Shiloh, Mt. Sinai and Mt. Vernon -- to name but a few.

To a greater extent than other industrialised democracies, the United States remains a Christian nation. That is despite, or perhaps because of, the separation of church and state laid down in the U.S. Constitution, which states: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."

Daniel Dreisbach, a professor at the American University in Washington, D.C., says: "By most external measures of religiosity, Americans are more religious than the people of virtually any other western democracy."
But most Americans appear content to keep their religion within the doors of their churches while enjoying all the comforts and temptations of a consumer society.
"While religion is highly popular, survey evidence suggests that it does not change people's lives to the degree one would expect from the level of professed faith," said pollster George Gallup Jr.

Shared belief in the same religion might be expected to impart a sense of unity and common purpose to Americans. Instead, it is a source of deep division, which some call a "culture war," between a secular-minded majority and fundamentalists, who are growing in numbers and power.
CULTURE WAR?

"We're in the midst of a culture war between traditionalists and secularism. It is out of this that we see the emergence of the religious right -- those who feel they were not consulted when it was decided that America was a mainly secular society," Dreisbach said.

Religion has been strong in America throughout its history. In his landmark study of U.S. democracy written in the 1830s, Alexis de Tocqueville called religion the most important political institution in the emerging nation.

Lacking formal recognition from the state, religious sects have had to compete in the free marketplace of ideas. They have done so with great success. In the United States today, nearly 500,000 churches, temples and other places of worship of all shapes and sizes dot the landscape.

There are some 2,000 denominations, plus countless independent churches and faith communities, some of which exist on the radio and television airwaves or in cyberspace. Seven of 10 Americans say they are church members. Americans donate billions of dollars to their churches each year and form about 90 percent of the world's Christian missionaries.
Many Americans believe this country was founded by God and has a special leadership role in the world. Politicians of both parties often invoke this belief.

"This is a nation founded by people fleeing religious persecution who believed America had a unique mission to be a beacon of justice and righteousness to the rest of the world," said Ralph Reed, outgoing director of the Christian Coalition, which has galvanised hundreds of thousands of conservative Christians for political action.
Gallup polls conducted in 1995 found that 96 percent of American adults believe in God or a universal spirit and 84 percent believe that Jesus is God or the son of God.
MORE BELIEVE IN HEAVEN THAN HELL

Other findings: 90 percent believe in heaven but only 73 percent in hell; 79 percent believe in miracles; 72 percent say there are angels and 46 percent believe that God created the world in six days, as described in Genesis.

Further, 90 percent of adults say they pray, 75 percent at least once a day. Some 43 percent said they attended church at least once during the seven days before the poll was taken; 58 percent say religion is very important in their lives and 30 percent say it is the most important part of their lives. As many as nine of 10 Americans say their lives have been touched in some way by Jesus.
Religion seems omnipresent in America. Sports stars thank Jesus for home runs hit and touchdowns scored. Politicians call for national days of prayer.
In Pensacola, Fla., thousands of people flock to a church where they believe they can experience the actual presence of God.
Four nights a week for the past two years, hundreds weep like babies, dance like dervishes or fall unconscious to the ground. So far, more than 1.5 million people have attended.

But television evangelist Pat Robertson is sceptical about the real faith of Americans. "It's a pop religion, not really based on religious standards. People say they want to have God, but often it's a God of convenience," he said.

Evangelical Christians say they are alienated by and at odds with many aspects of modern American society. Their efforts to force change on the majority have met with strong opposition both from secularists and more moderate Christians.

"Christianity is no longer the real faith of America. This is a sinful society. Violence, hate, bigotry, racism, murder of people both born and unborn -- we are a very sinful society," said Lew Weiden, a minister and ethics professor at Liberty University, a Baptist institution in Lynchburg.
PROTESTANT SHIFT

But many Christians believe such views are extreme. "American Protestantism is in the midst of a major shift. It is being split into two nearly (opposing) religions, both calling themselves Christianity," said Bruce Powers, author of a book on fundamentalism.
Powers sees two groups, one based in the South and West which holds to a literal, unbending reading of the Bible, and the other based in the North, with a more liberal view.

Fundamentalists are growing. While "mainstream Protestant" denominations were 40 percent of the nation in 1960, they are now barely more than 20 percent, according to research by John Green of the University of Akron.
Fundamentalist churches in the same period have recruited millions of new adherents and now claim around 26 percent of the population. Catholics have about the same proportion.

The culture war has manifested itself in bitter political battles over abortion, the role of women and homosexuals in society, school prayer, pornography and free speech, the content of television programmes -- even whether a judge in Alabama can post the Ten Commandments on the courtroom wall.
